title: A Shifting Global Currency Landscape
text:
A Shifting Global Currency Landscape

Louis-Vincent Gave, Romain Metivet

Gavekal Research
| 6 Aug 2026

A reserve currency has three attributes; it is (i) a medium of exchange, (ii) a reserve of value and (iii) a unit of account. For most of history, and until Richard Nixon’s 1971 suspension of the US dollar gold window, the “reserve of value” of dominant currencies was almost always dependent on some kind of link to gold (China first tried paper money in the Song dynasty, and France tried to back its “assignat currency” with confiscated church lands during the French Revolution, but neither experience was a happy one). In centuries past, one did not hold a claim on Byzantium, but rather gold that Byzantium had minted. Even the pound sterling of 1870—which came close to monopolizing all three above functions for the whole world—was merely an elegant receipt for gold into which sterling remained convertible. The same was true of the US dollar until 1971. Thus, in purely monetary terms, the past 55 years have been a genuinely unique experience in history; a time when the US dollar combined all three major functions for the entire globe, and this without the backing of a rare metal.
The US dollar managed this feat by making the greenback essential to buy oil. Instead of being gold backed, the US dollar became the petrodollar. Large oil exporters across the Middle East were essentially told it would be in their interest to (i) price their oil in US dollars and (ii) recycle their current account surpluses into US dollars. Any leader that departed from these simple instructions (whether Saddam Hussein in Iraq, Muammar Gaddafi in Libya, Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela….) would find their grip on power very ephemerous.
Which brings us to today. Recent events in the Middle East have suddenly put into question the post World War II bargain whereby Gulf countries agreed to US dollar domination, against the promise of total security from foreign, or domestic, threats. So could the sudden new Gulf security uncertainty prove enough to dethrone the petrodollar? Probably not, at least not for a while. History shows that when a currency starts to lose its preeminence, it is never the “medium of exchange” that fails first, nor the “unit of account”—invoicing habits tend to outlive the power that created them, sometimes by decades. Instead, it is the store-of-value function that quietly abandons the currency (usually in favor of gold). In that respect, the fact that central banks (including Middle Eastern central banks) have been purchasing a thousand tons of gold annually since 2022 obviously does raise eyebrows?
In this spirit, we propose to review over the following pages the important changes unfolding across the currency world today, and what these changes might mean for investments going forward.
1) Currencies as a means of exchange
An old Gavekal simile is that currencies are like computer operating systems. Both the US dollar and Microsoft Windows dominate their respective markets, and the fact that the US is home to both the world’s default currency, and its default operating system, are enormous comparative advantages. Rivals may emerge, but competing products need to be miles better for millions of people to abandon a familiar and comfortable system, regardless of its possible faults.
These twin advantages were turbocharged by decades of accelerating globalization, as the benefits offered by these systems become more valuable the more people used them. An established network is a terrific thing to own, if only because displacing it is almost impossible. A critical mass of new users is required for rival networks to compete effectively, and providing a marginally better service simply does not cut it. Without a growing user base, competing networks find it almost impossible to build the momentum necessary for accelerating adoption and economies of scale.
Yet, just like Apple eventually managed to build a parallel operating system to Microsoft, (perhaps not for everyone, but definitely for people working in design, architecture, marketing etc…), so is the renminbi slowly starting to build its own parallel circuit to the US dollar’s “means of exchange” rails.
To be clear, the “financial circuit”—covering foreign exchange, debt, collateral, and securities remains tied exclusively to the US dollar. And interestingly, it may be in the process of being reinvented, this time from the bottom-up. A merchant in Lagos wishing to flee the Nigerian naira may now choose to hold his cash reserves in USDT—the digital dollar issued by Tether, the largest stablecoin—while new US laws mandate that every token be backed by cash and short-term treasury bills. Tether thus reports a treasury exposure of roughly US$115-125bn—comparable to Saudi Arabia’s official holdings (a portfolio that took half a century to build, more on that later) but which Tether has amassed in just a few years. This would seem to show that the captive buyer of US debt has not vanished; he has simply shifted from the Saudi Arabian central bank (for example) to a multitude of individual investors across the Global South. Essentially, Tether is the Eurodollar reincarnated, with one crucial difference: this new version now comes with an American “kill switch” (Tether has already frozen over US$4bn at the request of the US Treasury).
At the same time, wherever China is the leading trading partner (basically every country in Asia, but also Africa, LatAm, Central Asia…), the “goods circuit” is shifting towards the renminbi. From nothing a decade ago, China now settles more trade in renminbi than it does in any other currency. This is happening not because anyone likes China per se, but because China’s trade is backed by “the world’s factory”. A currency that can buy everything being manufactured is more than sufficient for settling trade in goods, even if one cannot easily save the proceeds (the launch of the digital renminbi did fairly little to change that equation). All of which brings us to the next currency attribute.
2) Currencies as a store of value
As described in the introduction, one of the US dollar’s key supports over the past 55 years has been the willingness of energy-producing countries to price their oil in US dollars, and recycle their current account surpluses into US assets. What is amazing is that, in recent years, Middle Eastern countries have tended to recycle more than their surpluses into US assets. For example, over the past 12 months, it is estimated that the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, led by Saudi Arabia, have invested some US$66bn in the broader artificial intelligence ecosystem (i.e.: data centers, model developers etc…), almost all in the US. This has occurred even though Saudi Arabia registered a current account deficit through most of 2024 and 2025; a current account deficit which is now likely to get worse because of the Iran war and Strait of Hormuz closure.

Interactive chart
So when GCC countries promise US President Donald Trump to invest hundreds of billions of US dollars into the US, the various Gulf countries are no longer looking to recycle their energy rent. They are gearing up their balance sheets. Illustrating this is the chart below. Over the past decade, Saudi holdings of US treasuries have gone nowhere while simultaneously the Saudi government became one of the largest (non-American) issuers of US dollar debt globally.

Interactive chart
Saudi Arabia and some of the other GCC countries seem to have been gearing up to purchase American compute. This means that the Gulf has, in recent years, shifted from being a passive creditor (recycling energy earnings into purchases of US treasuries) to being leveraged shareholders—a far deeper form of dependency.
Meanwhile, four US companies are projecting capital expenditure of around US$725bn for 2026—nearly double the expected oil export revenues of all of Opec. All of which brings us to the obvious question of whether Washington is attempting to rebuild a new petrodollar, but this time with computing power, instead of oil, serving as the anchor? A “compute dollar” to replace a “petrodollar” which is slowly unraveling in front of our eyes?
This transition is perhaps all the more essential since the US dollar’s role as a store of value has been fundamentally undermined by the US’s repeated weaponization of its own currency (see BNP, Big Brother And The US Dollar). For many emerging market savers, the American “warehouse” now bears perhaps as great a risk of financial repression as their own domestic markets (see What Freezing Russia’s Reserves Means)?
Against that, the Chinese “workshop,” structurally, and very explicitly, forbids capital mobility. A country posting a current account surplus of over US$700bn is, by accounting identity, a net exporter of savings. For Chinese policymakers capital controls are not merely a barrier; they are the lock that secures the model. Opening the capital account would mean losing control over exchange rates in both directions—first through capital flight, then through equilibrium appreciation—spelling the possible death of the “workshop” in either scenario. A currency that is easy to earn but impossible to leave is a waiting room, not a store of value. Hence the defining monetary trend of the decade: the store-of-value function is reverting to gold, just as it did in 1914 and 1971.
In 2025, the Shanghai Gold Exchange opened offshore gold vaults in Hong Kong, with similar plans for Dubai and Riyadh in the works. These feature renminbi-denominated contracts and physical delivery—creating a de facto metallic exit route for renminbi holders, all without Beijing having to open its capital account. All of which helps the renminbi become a means of exchange, but still leaves the currency falling very short of being a store of value for non-Chinese investors.
3) Currencies as a unit of account
The “unit of account” role of currencies is the stickiest, and perhaps most underrated function of a currency. Today, oil remains priced in dollars even when settled in renminbi. More than half of global trade is invoiced in dollars. And this is precisely where the artificial intelligence battle mentioned above is playing out, for the US and Chinese AI strategies are mirror images of each other—as are their monetary implications.
In past pieces and video interviews, we have made the point that, American AI companies are fighting it out to build the very best possible “Ferrari” —rare, high-priced intelligence and US$2mn-a-year cloud contracts, all invoiced in dollars and settled via dollar rails, with every stablecoin payment mechanically funding a treasury bond.
Against that, China’s strategy has been to manufacture BYDs… and to give them away! These open models destroy the American invoice (see China Entrenches AI Competition) without creating a Chinese one. A free, or almost free, model generates no meaningful invoices in any currency. China’s 140trn or so daily tokens, sold at one-tenth to one-hundredth of the American price, carry virtually no monetary weight.
The implications are obvious enough: if, as per the above, the US is trying to transform the “petrodollar” into a “compute-dollar”, then these efforts are bound to fail given China’s “free AI” strategy. But this does not mean that China will create a “compute-renminbi”. Indeed, for the renminbi to gain ground, Beijing would have to sell compute in bundles: a free model tied to chips, data centers, and renminbi-based financing, settled through its own channels, with gold possibly serving as the exit route. Yet, China is clearly nowhere near able to deliver this today. And so a physical asymmetry seems to define the AI battlefield: America controls three-quarters of global compute capacity, yet faces a five-to-seven-year wait for grid connection. China adds the equivalent of Germany’s entire power grid annually, but struggles to fill its data centers due to a lack of chips. Each side possesses the very factor the other lacks.
This interdependence may also be getting worse and increasingly visible. The American infrastructure buildout itself now runs on Chinese equipment. Last year, the US imported over 8,000 transformers from China. The US also imported some 40% of its batteries… the “hostages” are thus already bolted into the substations.
Looking ahead, if we assume that, because of Chinese cost pressures, the bill for AI services will shrink for everyone—but that it will continue to be denominated in US dollars out of habit; that a company in, say, Brazil will run a Chinese model on Huawei chips—using a US model only at the margins—and will pay for it all in USDT (because the vendor itself wants payment in a currency people are moving away from), then the United States will lose the rent but keep the currency. Chinese-driven AI commoditization will drive a wedge between rent and currency, not between the US dollar and the renminbi. A free model destroys American rent without a single invoice being issued in renminbi.
4) Hong Kong’s growing importance
If this is the direction the world is heading into, then between these currencies, there must be passages. Which brings us to the importance of Hong Kong, the historical link between China and the rest of the world.
For most of its history, Hong Kong was a pipe or a bridge, bringing Western capital into China, and Chinese goods to the rest of the world. But in this new world, Hong Kong will likely evolve from being a pipe/bridge and will instead become a sluice where money no longer just passes through (with Hong Kong lawyers, bankers, accountants etc… taking a cut of course), but actually stays put.

Interactive chart
Hong Kong bank deposits grew by nearly 12% in 2025, almost entirely in foreign currency, and the city has now become the world’s leading center for cross-border wealth management. Mainland savings fleeing offshore end up there precisely because it is the place least exposed to both systems simultaneously. As with the Eurodollar, the stock that stays there inflates the local monetary base and puts downward pressure on interest rates. In the spring of 2025, the monetary authority had to buy nearly US$17bn to weaken the Hong Kong dollar, which had been pushed to its ceiling by inflows from the mainland. The Hibor collapsed toward 0% while the Federal Reserve’s rate was above 4%...
In time, this will drive asset prices through liquidity, not through profits. The precedent here might be London, a city that grew ever richer for 50 years thanks to its similar role as a sluice (for Russian savings, for Arab savings, for the savings of rich Europeans…) and this without the value of its stock market increasing very much.
In this framework, the Hong Kong dollar peg is the load-bearing wall of the sluice. And notice where Beijing has placed its gold vault: inside it. Savings held in Hong Kong have fled the jurisdiction, but not yet the paper. The vault of the Shanghai Gold Exchange, a few streets away from the deposits, offers savers the final step, the one that leads from currency to metal without ever entering either Chinese, or American, systems. The sluice is the antechamber of the store of value; what stops there ultimately chooses between circulating, or becoming petrified.
If this analysis is right, then Hong Kong becomes the most strategic, and perhaps contested asset in the system (the decision by the US consular staff in Hong Kong to very publicly meet with Hong Kong student leaders at the height of the 2019 riots was perhaps more than just a massive breach of diplomatic decorum?). And sure, there are other sluices (i.e.: Singapore, Dubai…), but none that straddle so perfectly the Chinese world and the US world.
At each transition from one system to another, a toll is paid: Hong Kong, gold vaults, and stablecoins are the locks where value comes to a halt. And what makes the arrangement sustainable is that each party finds in it exactly what its regime needs:

China retains its surpluses, and therefore employment and social peace, without ever opening its capital account.
The United States retains the unit of account, captive demand for treasury bonds, and partial reindustrialization financed by the factories of others.
Gold offers China’s partners the exit strategy the renminbi cannot provide. More importantly, gold allows both superpowers to distrust each other, without causing the system to collapse.

The value of Hong Kong is thus that of a toll—it grows with the traffic between the three currencies (gold, US dollar and renminbi), that is, with mistrust itself. The more the world fragments, the more profitable the crossing points become. As long as Chinese savings continue to flee, Hong Kong will see its liquidity swell and its rates decouple downwards from the Fed.
If the framework holds, the macroeconomic consequences will follow. First, on the American curve: short and long positions cease to obey the same logic. Short positions now have a structural buyer insensitive to price, since each stablecoin issued is a treasury bond automatically purchased; long positions have only natural sellers, as central banks shift to gold and GCC savings to equity. The curve must therefore steepen structurally, not in anticipation of inflation but through a divorce between two customer groups; and the day when we reach a ceiling along the way, through curve control or regulatory constraint, it will be an admission that financial repression has begun, and the signal of the final migration towards gold. Or perhaps the renminbi.
5) Conclusion
There is no longer, at the global level, a currency that fulfills all three functions, and there will likely not be one for a very long time. There are today three currencies linked by sluices, and history dictates the order of division.

The medium of exchange is splitting. The US dollar retains financial circulation, debt, foreign exchange, and stablecoins. The renminbi is slowly taking over the payment for goods, because a currency backed by the world’s factory is more than sufficient to pay for goods.
The store of value is abandoning the US dollar; it is returning to gold.
The unit of account, the stickiest, remains American; it is the last bastion. Which is why the battle over AI billing could prove very important.

None of this is bullish for long-dated bonds, or for the US dollar. This new set-up is bullish for gold. But most of all, it might be very bullish Hong Kong assets.
